projects.content_zh: 陕西是我国石窟发展比较发达的地区之一，以晚期石窟为主。目前共发现北魏至明、清时期石窟350余处，其中比较重要的石窟：北朝9处，隋、唐、五代32处，宋、金、元73处。陕西石窟中大型窟少，小型窟多；群体窟少，单体窟多；大体量造像少，小体量造像多；北朝、隋、唐石窟少，宋代石窟较多；长期连续造窟的窟少，时代单一的窟多；关中及陕南的窟少，陕北的窟多；题材组合复杂的少，题材简单的多。北朝石窟有宜君县的秦家河、花石崖、福地、苜蓿沟、彭村，安塞县的剑化寺、云山品寺，黄陵县的双龙香坊，甘泉县的老君寺，彬县的大佛寺等处，北魏时代占多数。这个时期石窟的龛、窟难分，规模较小，佛龛进深很浅，面宽与高度多在1米左右。佛龛多为拱形或尖拱形，有的龛侧饰连结柱。造像主要为一佛二菩萨，或有飞天和胡服供养人。开凿于西魏大统元年（公元535年）的宜君福地石窟，除刻有佛教造像外，还雕有道教天尊像，发愿文中的供养者称道士、道民，是迄今发现最早有纪年的佛、道合龛造像。隋、唐石窟众多，有蓝田之佛寺重兴，铜川的金锁关，宜君的焦寨，安塞的大佛寺、黑泉驿，富县的石泓寺、川庄，甘泉的孟家河、方家河、刘老庄，吴旗的石空寺，洛川的史家河，韩城的七佛洞、开化寺、朝阳洞，佳县的玉皇寺，靖边的千佛寺等处。宋、金、元各代石窟主要分布在陕北延安市，这与宋王朝大力倡导佛教以及宋与西夏之间的战事有着密切关系。宋太祖建隆元年（公元960年），太祖继位数月，即解除后周毁佛之令，佛寺重兴。尤其以安塞、甘泉、子长、富县、延安等处最为密集，不仅石窟数量多，而且技法纯熟，题材也更趋世俗化，尤以子长县钟山石窟、富县阁子头石窟、黄陵县双龙石窟以及延安市万佛洞石窟最具代表性。彬县大佛寺石窟位于彬县城西10公里处的泾河南岸的水帘洞乡大佛寺村附近的清凉山上，是陕西省境内规模最大的石窟群，也是中国现存初唐时期和盛唐时期规模最大、最为精美的石窟群之一。1988年公布为全国第三批重点文物保护单位。大佛寺石窟始凿于南北朝时期，大规模开凿于唐初，贞观二年（公元628年）基本建成，原名应福寺，乃唐太宗为了给对抗薛举、薛仁杲大战中阵亡将士应福而建。北宋仁宗皇帝为其养母刘太后举国庆寿时，改名庆寿寺。人们因其佛像高大雄伟，从明景泰年间俗称大佛寺并沿用。大佛寺石窟群坐南面北，依山凿窟，雕石成像，沿东西方向排列在陡峭垂直的崖面上。现存大小窟龛361个，其中洞窟107个，佛龛254个，有造像的洞窟共19个，造像1498躯，错落有致地分布于约400米长的立体崖面上，分为大佛窟、千佛洞、罗汉洞（佛洞）、丈八佛窟、僧房窟五部分。石窟群以大佛洞为全寺的中心，可以分为三大部分：中部、西部、东部。中部为整个石窟群的主体部分，包括大佛洞及紧邻两侧的千佛洞和罗汉洞，共12窟，称之为中崖，即明镜台；西部窟室有些还保留了部分造像，共8窟，称之为西崖；东部的窟室均无造像，也无任何石刻碑文，平面多为方形，有少数圆形和椭圆形的窟室，共87窟，称之为东崖。东部的窟室有单一窟室、一窟双室以及一窟四室等不同类型，有些窟室的入口上方还有采光用的窗口，这些窟室的规模都不大，且各窟室外在崖壁上还可以看到为了互相联系而架设木栈道所留在崖壁上的孔洞痕迹。其中，东崖和中崖洞窟比较密集。开凿较早、规模最大和保存最为完整的是大佛窟，其次是千佛洞和罗汉洞，其大约开凿于唐高宗执政时期。大佛窟完工于贞观二年（公元628年），是我国现存唐太宗时期规模最大、最为精美的一处洞窟。洞窟南北长18米，东西宽34.5米，高31（24）米，方向为北偏东15度。洞窟内平面近似半圆形，洞窟上部的总体构造为穹隆形。洞窟前有砖木结构的五层楼阁屹立，可以登临眺望。洞内共有70龛，1001躯造像。洞正中有石雕佛像三尊，阿弥陀佛居中，观音菩萨侍左，大势至菩萨侍右，均为石胎泥塑。阿弥陀佛高27米，宽10米，佛指长2米。依岩跌坐，肩宽宽厚，披衣袒胸，腰系佩带，造型自然丰满，神情端庄，颇显唐代风格，大佛寺亦因此佛而得名。大佛背光边沿浮雕飞舞在碧空的22躯飞天伎乐，花纹装饰精美，充分表现了初唐的艺术风格。观音菩萨高21.5米，大势至菩萨高21米。大佛洞内四壁布满佛龛，雕刻大小佛像、菩萨像400余尊，列置最小的仅2厘米。大佛窟规模宏大，造像雄伟，雕刻精致，是古代造像艺术中的一大宝库。从形制来看，大佛窟主大像窟继承了公元4、5世纪佛教自印度传入中国早期时，新疆克孜尔石窟马蹄形平面并主像身后两侧凿出礼拜隧道的做法。从结构来看，大佛窟顶部采用了敦煌莫高窟中最为流行的木构房屋的横向人字披形式。从雕刻手法来看，大佛身后的背光雕刻，显示出北朝的佛教艺术传统。罗汉洞位于大佛窟西侧，大约开凿于唐高宗时期，共有4个石窟，规模较小。第三窟内壁有浮雕经变故事60余幅，并保存有唐宋以来游人题刻甚多。其余三窟内，均有石雕和菩萨造像，数量不等，造型与大佛窟相似，雕工细致。千佛洞位于罗汉洞东侧10号窟，大约开凿于唐高宗时期，外观是一明两暗的厅堂，内为石窟。窟内均有佛和菩萨造像，四周墙壁遍布浮雕，共计300余幅，刻画的题材为人物和经变故事，惟妙惟肖。千佛洞有十几处佛龛均包含着明确的铭文发愿题记，大部分是在武则天执政时期雕造出来的。这个时期的造像都具有健美的身材、婀娜多姿的体态，体现了大唐帝国中最为纯正的佛教造像艺术。特别是在千佛洞中还保存了一处与真人等高的一佛二菩萨造像龛，这处等身像龛的佛与菩萨，是集人体的写实美、夸张美于一体的雕刻艺术，也是千佛洞武则天时期雕刻的代表作品，是最为典型的初唐长安风格的造像艺术。丈八佛窟又称应福寺，是大佛寺年代最早的佛窟，位于大佛窟以西200米处，沿山开凿的9孔小石窟散布在崖面上。窟内有依山雕刻的一佛二菩萨站立像，系典型的石胎泥塑造像，肃穆庄重，俊美优雅，具有明显的北周佛教造像艺术特征，显示该窟开凿于南北朝时期。慈善寺石窟位于宝鸡市麟游县城东6公里处漆水河西南岸的崖面之上。石窟开凿于隋仁寿年间（公元601至604年），唐高宗永徽四年（公元654年）又进行大规模续建。石窟内佛像丰满圆润，刀法洗练，代表了隋唐时期佛造像的最高艺术水平。它的建筑和雕刻样式曾是当时建造石窟的范本，因而保存下来的洞窟建筑也十分珍贵。2001年公布为第五批全国重点文物保护单位。陕西宝鸡麟游是隋唐帝王避暑的行宫九成宫所在地，慈善寺是当时皇帝后妃及大臣在麟游避暑时礼佛的宫廷寺院。唐文宗开成元年（公元836年）慈善寺佛舍遭大水毁坏，后多次修复。现存石窟分布于高28米的崖壁上，西崖有三大窟，南崖有窟龛多座，两处共有12个洞窟，6座佛龛，47尊造像。西崖第一、二窟平面呈马蹄形，窟内佛像体量较大。从北向南依次编号1至3号窟，第一窟主佛高5.5米，即为隋代开凿镌造。隋代存在时间短促，所遗佛教文物较少，像慈善寺第一窟主佛这样高大完整、保存到今天的隋皇宫石窟造像，极为珍贵。南崖上有9个摩崖造像龛，内凿佛像，体量较小，不规则地呈东西向排列，尺寸大小不一，且无统一的布局规划。此外，慈善寺石窟窟壁内外还保留有唐代至明代的题记、刻经5处。慈善寺石窟属于前殿后佛的平面布局，与彬县大佛寺的形制相同，但规模不如前者。这种窟的形制，佛像较大，常占据窟内主要空间，而礼佛活动主要在窟外大殿中进行。1号窟位于西崖的最北面，平面为马蹄形，窟顶近于穹隆，中部平整。窟室内部空间较大，而在窟口处收缩。窟门上部呈圆拱状，已经崩塌，仅南部顶上拐角处保存一小部分弧度，推测窟门原应是拱形。窟门高6.72米，宽4.45米，进深5.90米。窟内依西（后）、北、南壁下部凿有倒凹字形坛，西坛高1.5、侧坛高0.9米，西坛向外伸出构成主佛下座。坛上依三壁各雕一结跏跌坐佛像。2号窟位于慈善寺西崖北部1号窟南侧，北距1号窟9.5米。平面呈马蹄形，两侧壁外弧，窟口内收。窟口残损，原应为圆形拱。窟高538米、窟门宽3.20米、后壁宽3.76米，窟中部最宽5.30米、进深2米。倚着西壁雕一立佛，左右壁下部各开一大龛，上部各开一小龛。左壁大龛内雕一佛二菩萨像，右壁大龛内雕一佛二弟子。2号窟主佛南侧下距地面0.96米处，刻有佛经一部，高1.30米、宽0.65米许，楷书，字1.5至2厘米见方，共31行。经中有许多字已漫漶不清，仅可辨识的字就有一千余言，无疑可大大地弥补敦煌残卷之缺。敬福经可以堪称为迄今为止发现的全国现存刻写时间最早，保存字数最多，内容最完整的世俗佛经。3号窟位于北崖2号窟南侧1.5米处，仅仅开凿了窟口，便废弃了。从现存遗迹上看，窟口略成弧顶横长方形，窟内平面呈长方形。窟高4.9米、窟门宽6.17米、进深1.8米，窟口下沿距地面1.9米。窟室后壁中部有后代补凿的佛龛造像，虽承唐风，但造型较为呆板，手法拙劣。慈善寺石窟总面积不大，只有两座庙，但特别可贵的是，这尊大佛因未经后代装修，仍保持了初盛唐时代的雕刻特点，反映了初盛唐雕刻造像的雄浑而又精美细致的高超手法，其所雕佛像，头部稍大，肌肤丰满，神态完美，裙带衣纹流畅，刀法简练有力，时代风格鲜明，是隋唐皇家寺院佛教艺术的精品之作。富县石泓寺石窟又名川子河石窟，位于延安市富县城西65公里处的直罗镇川子河北岸。石窟依崖凿石而成，2006年公布为第六批全国重点文物保护单位。从窟内题记看，此窟始凿于隋大业年间（公元605至618年），唐、宋、金、明、清各代都有雕凿，其大多数开凿于唐、宋时期。解县石泓寺，开凿时代在唐初或更早一些，最突出的是金代开凿的窟，大小雕像三千多尊。窟前有清代修建民国修复的皇经楼，上刻石泓寺三个大字，寺前现有三开间寺楼1座及12间配房。石泓寺坐东北面西南，选址优越。石窟南面与石山对峙，中间形成200米宽的东西峡谷，川子河从西向东由窟前流过，这里环境优美，风景宜人，是佛教徒修行的好地方。石窟依崖而凿，在东西长约70米的山崖上共分布10个洞窟，其中7个有石刻造像，共计小龛65个，石造像3371尊。石窟平面布置上均采用中央佛坛背屏式，窟室与窟口之间不设甬道，平面呈方形，窟口仿木结构做法，雕出檐柱及阑额。7座石窟中年代较早的是中间的5号窟，其余依次为3号窟、2号窟和4号窟，最外侧的石窟开凿年代较晚，说明各代凿窟均在已有洞窟的两侧进行，属于分布集中、时代连续的石窟群。5号窟为隋大业年间（公元605至618年）题记，窟口为长方形，窟内面宽2.5米、深3米、高2.1米，中央佛坛起背屏，供一佛二菩萨，东西壁共有造像34尊。2号窟、3号窟和4号窟的形制相似，窟门呈长方形，两间雕成门楣抱框，窟内平面为长方形，进深大于面宽，窟顶微微凸起，室中央起佛帐，佛像后部均做背屏直通窟顶，背屏和窟内侧壁上有各种造像。以上三窟的最早题记分别为2号窟北宋开宝二年（公元969年）、3号窟唐咸通五年（公元860年）、4号窟后周显德元年（公元954年）。6号窟规模最大，造像众多，窟内有甬道，对进深较大的窟室来讲，甬道起到了稳定结构的作用。窟室平面近方形，面阔10.3米、进深10.65米、高5.35米，中央布置佛坛，有一佛二菩萨二弟子，佛与菩萨均结跏跌坐于莲花座上，二弟子分立两旁。佛坛背屏演变成了四根通顶连地的造像柱，加强了视觉的纵深感。石柱上雕刻造像1131尊，窟室两壁有造像1947尊，窟顶刻有几何图案花纹。造像铭刻最早的年代是金皇统元年（1141年）。在造像内容和雕刻技法上比唐宋时期更广泛、更活泼。1号窟和7号窟均凿于明代，窟中表现的是佛、道、儒三教合一的内容，在技法上均逊于其他的几个窟，可以看出至明代，造窟之风衰颓。窟内中央不再设佛坛，而将佛坛放到窟室的后壁，人物造像神形刻板，内容芜杂。米脂万佛洞原名万福洞，位于米脂县城北8公里处的无定河右岸悬崖之上，是陕北地区洞窟最多，规模最大的石窟群。1982年列为县级文物保护单位。万佛洞建造年代尚不可考，一般认为建于宋至明初。洞窟选址险要，悬崖顺无定河为南北向，横长约500米许，崖顶平坦，崖层距地面约20米，至崖顶约20至30米。悬崖峭壁，怪石嶙峋，顶层向外突出，其状险峻。万佛洞倚崖而建，主要有伽蓝护法殿、观音洞、灵宫殿、白衣洞、关王洞、九天圣母洞，现存窟内大部造像被毁。主窟伽蓝护法殿，平面呈方形，宽8米，进深11.6米，高4.7米，窟顶前部有平棋15格，内有浮雕花草、瑞兽等图案，后半部中心为穹隆顶，中为八卦，外围浮雕一周小佛造像等。窟正面下凿成长方形石坛基，上有3个须弥座，两侧各有一长方形石坛基。窟中有两根长方形石柱，直达窟顶，南北两面宽约1.30米，东西两面宽约1米，上雕刻小佛及题记，在柱中部岩石断层不宜雕像处，改用彩绘。窟两壁凿刻形态各异、造型多样的小佛，间以题记。正面与南北两面有浮雕佛像，里面无佛像。南柱正面，有横向排列的浮雕佛像15排，计有佛像130尊，其中上部有大肚佛一尊，下部佛像为盘坐，高约0.2米、底座宽0.1米，小佛像高0.5米、底座宽0.1米。南柱北面，上部有佛像9排，每排有横向排列的浮雕佛像17尊，计有佛像153尊，下部有佛像7排，每排有横向排列的浮雕佛像11尊，计有佛像77尊。南柱南面，计有佛像18排，每排有横向排列的浮雕佛像16尊，计有佛像288尊。北柱正面，有横向排列的浮雕佛像17排，上部1至9排每排13尊，下部10至17排，每排8尊，计有佛像181尊。北柱南面与南柱北面佛像的排数与尊数基本相同，计有佛像230尊。北柱北面，有横向排列的浮雕佛像16排，每排有佛像11尊、13尊、17尊、12尊不等，计有佛像217尊。洞窟内的正壁，有横向排列的浮雕佛像12排，每排120尊，每排每尊位置上下交错，计有佛像1440尊。洞窟内的北壁，有横向排列的浮雕佛像18排，每排有佛像147尊，计有佛像2646尊。洞窟内的南壁，有横向排列的浮雕佛像19排，每排有佛像150尊，计有佛像2850尊。
projects.content_en: Shaanxi is one of the regions with relatively developed grotto development in China, mainly featuring late-period grottoes. Currently, more than 350 grottoes from the Northern Wei to Ming and Qing dynasties have been discovered, among which the more important grottoes include: 9 from the Northern Dynasties, 32 from Sui, Tang, and Five Dynasties, and 73 from Song, Jin, and Yuan. In Shaanxi grottoes, there are few large caves and many small caves; few group caves and many single caves; few large-scale statues and many small-scale statues; few Northern Dynasties, Sui, and Tang grottoes and many Song grottoes; few grottoes with continuous carving over long periods and many grottoes of a single era; few grottoes in Guanzhong and southern Shaanxi and many in northern Shaanxi; few with complex subject combinations and many with simple subjects. Northern Dynasties grottoes include Qinjiahe, Huashiya, Fudi, Muxugou, and Pengcun in Yijun County; Jianhua Temple and Yunshan Pin Temple in Ansai County; Shuanglong Xiangfang in Huangling County; Laojun Temple in Ganquan County; and the Great Buddha Temple in Bin County, with the Northern Wei era accounting for the majority. During this period, the niches and caves of grottoes were difficult to distinguish, with small scales; the Buddhist niches had very shallow depths, with face widths and heights mostly around 1 m. Buddhist niches were mostly arched or pointed-arched, with some niches having connecting columns on the sides. The statues were mainly one Buddha and two bodhisattvas, or with flying apsaras and Hu-costume donors. The Yijun Fudi Grotto, carved in the 1st year of Datong, Western Wei (535 AD), in addition to Buddhist statues, also carved Taoist Tianzun (Celestial Venerable) statues, with the donors in the dedication inscriptions calling themselves 'daoshi' (Taoist priests) and 'daomin' (Taoist people), making it the earliest dated Buddha-Taoist combined niche statue discovered to date. Sui and Tang grottoes are numerous, including the revived Buddhist temple in Lantian, Jinsuoguan in Tongchuan, Jiaozhai in Yijun, Great Buddha Temple and Heiquanyi in Ansai, Shihong Temple and Chuanzhuang in Fuxian, Mengjiahe, Fangjiahe, and Liulaozhuang in Ganquan, Shikong Temple in Wuqi, Shijiahe in Luochuan, Qifo Cave, Kaihua Temple, and Chaoyang Cave in Hancheng, Yuhuang Temple in Jiaxian, and Qianfo Temple in Jingbian. Song, Jin, and Yuan grottoes are mainly distributed in Yan'an City, northern Shaanxi, which is closely related to the Song dynasty's vigorous promotion of Buddhism and the wars between Song and Western Xia. In the 1st year of Jianlong, Emperor Taizu of Song (960 AD), just a few months after ascending the throne, Emperor Taizu lifted the Later Zhou decree destroying Buddhism, and Buddhist temples revived. Especially in Ansai, Ganquan, Zichang, Fuxian, and Yan'an, the grottoes are most dense; not only are there many grottoes, but the techniques are also mature, and the subjects tend to be more secularized, with the Zhongshan Grotto in Zichang County, Gezitou Grotto in Fuxian County, Shuanglong Grotto in Huangling County, and Wanfo Cave Grotto in Yan'an City being the most representative. The Bin County Great Buddha Temple Grottoes are located on Qingliang Mountain near Dafosi Village, Shuidongdong Township, on the south bank of the Jing River, 10 km west of Bin County town. It is the largest grotto group in Shaanxi Province and one of the largest and most exquisite grotto groups from the early Tang and high Tang periods existing in China. It was designated as the third batch of National Key Cultural Heritage Sites in 1988. The Great Buddha Temple Grottoes were first carved during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period, with large-scale carving in the early Tang, basically completed in the 2nd year of Zhenguan (628 AD). Originally named Yingfu Temple, it was built by Emperor Taizong of Tang to bring blessings to the soldiers who died in the battle against Xue Ju and Xue Rengao. When Emperor Renzong of Northern Song celebrated the birthday of his adoptive mother Empress Dowager Liu across the empire, it was renamed Qingshou Temple. Because of its tall and majestic Buddha statues, people commonly called it the Great Buddha Temple from the Jingtai period of Ming and this name has been used ever since. The Great Buddha Temple Grotto group faces north with its back to south, carving caves into the mountain and carving statues from stone, arranged along the east-west direction on steep vertical cliff faces. Currently, there are 361 large and small caves and niches, including 107 caves and 254 Buddhist niches; there are 19 caves with statues in total, with 1,498 statue bodies, distributed in an orderly manner on a three-dimensional cliff face about 400 m long, divided into five parts: Great Buddha Cave, Thousand-Buddha Cave, Arhat Cave (Buddha Cave), Zhangba Buddha Cave, and Monk Room Caves. The grotto group centers on the Great Buddha Cave as the core of the entire temple and can be divided into three major parts: central, western, and eastern. The central part is the main part of the entire grotto group, including the Great Buddha Cave and the adjacent Thousand-Buddha Cave and Arhat Cave on both sides, totaling 12 caves, called the 'Central Cliff,' i.e., the Mirror Platform; the western cave chambers still retain some statues, totaling 8 caves, called the 'West Cliff'; the eastern cave chambers have no statues and no stone inscriptions, mostly square in plane, with a few circular and oval cave chambers, totaling 87 caves, called the 'East Cliff.' The eastern cave chambers include different types such as single cave chambers, one-cave double-chamber, and one-cave four-chamber; some cave chambers have lighting windows above the entrances; these cave chambers are not large in scale, and on the cliff outside each cave chamber, traces of holes left by wooden walkways erected for mutual connection can still be seen. Among them, the East Cliff and Central Cliff caves are relatively dense. The earliest carved, largest-scale, and best-preserved cave is the Great Buddha Cave, followed by the Thousand-Buddha Cave and Arhat Cave, which were approximately carved during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of Tang. The Great Buddha Cave was completed in the 2nd year of Zhenguan (628 AD), making it the largest and most exquisite cave from the reign of Emperor Taizong of Tang existing in China. The cave is 18 m long north-south, 34.5 m wide east-west, and 31 (24) m high, oriented 15 degrees east of north. The interior plane of the cave is approximately semicircular, and the overall structure of the upper part of the cave is dome-shaped. In front of the cave, a five-story brick-wood structure pavilion stands, allowing climbing and viewing. Inside the cave, there are 70 niches and 1,001 statue bodies. In the center of the cave, there are three stone-carved Buddha statues: Amitabha Buddha in the center, Guanyin Bodhisattva on the left, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva on the right, all of stone-clay construction. Amitabha Buddha is 27 m high and 10 m wide, with a Buddha finger 2 m long. Sitting cross-legged against the rock, with broad shoulders, robes draping and chest exposed, a waist sash, a naturally plump form, and a dignified expression, quite showing the Tang style; the Great Buddha Temple is also named after this Buddha. On the edge of the Great Buddha's halo, 22 flying apsara musicians are relief-carved dancing in the blue sky, with exquisitely decorated patterns, fully expressing the artistic style of the early Tang. Guanyin Bodhisattva is 21.5 m high, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva is 21 m high. The four walls inside the Great Buddha Cave are covered with Buddhist niches, carving more than 400 large and small Buddha and bodhisattva statues, with the smallest being only 2 cm. The Great Buddha Cave is grand in scale, with majestic statues and exquisite carvings, making it a great treasure house of ancient statue art. In terms of form, the Great Buddha Cave's main large statue cave inherits the practice of the Kizil Grottoes in Xinjiang from the 4th and 5th centuries, when Buddhism was first introduced to China from India—horse-shoe-shaped plane with worship tunnels carved on both sides behind the main statue. In terms of structure, the top of the Great Buddha Cave adopts the most popular horizontal herringbone roof form of wooden buildings in the Mogao Grottoes at Dunhuang. In terms of carving techniques, the halo carving behind the Great Buddha shows the Buddhist art tradition of the Northern Dynasties. The Arhat Cave is located west of the Great Buddha Cave, approximately carved during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of Tang, with a total of 4 grottoes, small in scale. The inner wall of the third cave has more than 60 relief-carved sutra illustration stories, and preserves many inscriptions by visitors since the Tang and Song dynasties. In the remaining three caves, there are stone-carved and bodhisattva statues of varying quantities, with forms similar to the Great Buddha Cave and exquisite carving. The Thousand-Buddha Cave is located in Cave No. 10 east of the Arhat Cave, approximately carved during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of Tang; its exterior is a hall with one bright and two dark bays, with grottoes inside. Inside the cave, there are Buddha and bodhisattva statues, and the surrounding walls are covered with relief carvings, totaling more than 300, depicting subjects of figures and sutra illustration stories, vivid and lifelike. The Thousand-Buddha Cave has more than ten Buddhist niches all containing clear dedication inscriptions, most carved during the reign of Wu Zetian. The statues from this period all have vigorous figures and graceful postures, reflecting the purest Buddhist statue art of the Great Tang Empire. Especially in the Thousand-Buddha Cave, a one-Buddha-two-bodhisattva statue niche at human height is preserved; the Buddha and bodhisattvas in this life-size niche are a carving art integrating realistic beauty and exaggerated beauty of the human body, and are also representative works carved during the Wu Zetian period in the Thousand-Buddha Cave, being the most typical early Tang Chang'an-style statue art. The Zhangba Buddha Cave, also called Yingfu Temple, is the earliest Buddhist cave at the Great Buddha Temple, located 200 m west of the Great Buddha Cave, with 9 small grottoes carved along the mountain scattered on the cliff face. Inside the cave, there are one Buddha and two bodhisattva standing statues carved against the mountain, typical stone-clay statues, solemn and dignified, handsome and elegant, with obvious Northern Zhou Buddhist statue art characteristics, indicating that this cave was carved during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period. The Cishan Temple Grottoes are located on the cliff face on the southwest bank of the Qi River, 6 km east of Linyou County town, Baoji City. The grottoes were carved during the Renshou period of Sui (601-604 AD), and large-scale additional construction was carried out in the 4th year of Yonghui, Emperor Gaozong of Tang (654 AD). The Buddha statues inside the grottoes are plump and rounded, with refined carving techniques, representing the highest artistic level of Buddha statues in the Sui-Tang period. Its architectural and carving styles were once the models for building grottoes at that time, so the preserved cave architecture is also very precious. It was designated as the fifth batch of National Key Cultural Heritage Sites in 2001. Linyou in Baoji, Shaanxi, is the location of the Jiucheng Palace, the summer palace of Sui-Tang emperors; Cishan Temple was the court temple where emperors, empresses, and ministers worshipped Buddha during their summer stays in Linyou. In the 1st year of Kaicheng, Emperor Wenzong of Tang (836 AD), the Cishan Temple Buddhist hall was destroyed by flood, and was repaired multiple times afterwards. The existing grottoes are distributed on a cliff 28 m high, with three large caves on the west cliff and many cave niches on the south cliff; the two places have a total of 12 caves, 6 Buddhist niches, and 47 statues. The first and second caves on the west cliff have horse-shoe-shaped planes, with large Buddha statues inside. Numbered 1 to 3 from north to south, the main Buddha of Cave 1 is 5.5 m high, carved during the Sui dynasty. The Sui dynasty existed for a short time, leaving few Buddhist cultural relics; a Sui imperial palace grotto statue as tall, complete, and preserved to today as the main Buddha of Cave 1 at Cishan Temple is extremely precious. On the south cliff, there are 9 cliff statue niches with Buddha statues carved inside, small in scale, irregularly arranged east-west, with varying sizes and no unified layout plan. In addition, inside and outside the cave walls of Cishan Temple Grottoes, 5 inscriptions and carved scriptures from the Tang to Ming dynasties are preserved. The Cishan Temple Grottoes belong to the 'front hall, rear Buddha' plane layout, same as the form of the Great Buddha Temple in Bin County, but smaller in scale. In this cave form, the Buddha statue is large, often occupying the main space inside the cave, while Buddhist worship activities mainly take place in the hall outside the cave. Cave 1 is located at the northernmost part of the west cliff, with a horse-shoe-shaped plane; the cave top is nearly dome-shaped, flat in the middle. The interior space of the cave chamber is large, while contracting at the cave entrance. The upper part of the cave door is round-arched, having collapsed, with only a small part of the arc preserved at the top corner on the south side; it is推测 that the cave door should originally have been arched. The cave door is 6.72 m high, 4.45 m wide, and 5.90 m deep. Inside the cave, along the lower parts of the west (rear), north, and south walls, an inverted-concave-shaped altar is carved; the west altar is 1.5 m high and the side altars are 0.9 m high, with the west altar extending outward to form the main Buddha's lower seat. On the altar, along each of the three walls, one cross-legged sitting Buddha statue is carved. Cave 2 is located south of Cave 1 on the northern part of the west cliff, 9.5 m north of Cave 1. Its plane is horse-shoe-shaped, with both side walls curving outward and the cave entrance contracting inward. The cave entrance is damaged, originally should have been a round arch. The cave is 5.38 m high, the cave door is 3.20 m wide, the rear wall is 3.76 m wide, the widest part in the middle of the cave is 5.30 m, and the depth is 2 m. A standing Buddha is carved against the west wall; the lower parts of the left and right walls each have a large niche, and the upper parts each have a small niche. Inside the large niche on the left wall, one Buddha and two bodhisattva statues are carved; inside the large niche on the right wall, one Buddha and two disciples are carved. On the south side of the main Buddha in Cave 2, 0.96 m above the ground, a Buddhist scripture is carved, 1.30 m high and about 0.65 m wide, in regular script, with characters 1.5 to 2 cm square, totaling 31 lines. Many characters in the scripture have become blurred and illegible, with only more than a thousand characters discernible, which can undoubtedly greatly弥补 the gaps in the Dunhuang fragmentary scrolls. The Jingfu Sutra can be called the earliest-dated, most-character-preserving, and most-complete secular Buddhist scripture existing in the country discovered to date. Cave 3 is located 1.5 m south of Cave 2 on the north cliff; only the cave entrance was carved before it was abandoned. From the existing remains, the cave entrance is slightly arc-topped and horizontally rectangular, and the interior plane of the cave is rectangular. The cave is 4.9 m high, the cave door is 6.17 m wide, the depth is 1.8 m, and the lower edge of the cave entrance is 1.9 m above the ground. In the middle of the rear wall of the cave chamber, there is a later-carved Buddhist niche statue, although following the Tang style, the form is relatively stiff and the technique is crude. The total area of Cishan Temple Grottoes is not large, with only two temples, but what is particularly valuable is that this Great Buddha, because it has not been renovated by later generations, still maintains the carving characteristics of the early and high Tang periods, reflecting the vigorous and exquisite techniques of early and high Tang carved statues; the carved Buddha statues have slightly larger heads, plump skin, perfect expressions, flowing robe and sash patterns, and powerful and concise carving techniques, with a distinct era style, making them fine works of Buddhist art of Sui-Tang royal temples. The Fuxian Shihong Temple Grottoes, also called Chuanzi River Grottoes, are located on the north bank of the Chuanzi River, Zhiluo Town, 65 km west of Fuxian County town, Yan'an City. The grottoes are carved into the cliff, and were designated as the sixth batch of National Key Cultural Heritage Sites in 2006. From the inscriptions inside the caves, these grottoes were first carved during the Daye period of Sui (605-618 AD), with carvings in the Tang, Song, Jin, Ming, and Qing dynasties, most carved during the Tang and Song periods. The Shihong Temple in Xie County, its carving era was in the early Tang or earlier, with the most prominent being the caves carved in the Jin dynasty, with more than three thousand large and small statues. In front of the caves, there is a Huangjing Tower built in the Qing dynasty and repaired in the Republic period, with the three characters 'Shihong Temple' carved on it; in front of the temple, there is currently a three-bay temple tower and 12 side rooms. Shihong Temple faces southwest with its back to northeast, with an excellent site selection. The south side of the grottoes faces a stone mountain, forming an east-west gorge 200 m wide in the middle, with the Chuanzi River flowing from west to east in front of the caves; the environment here is beautiful and the scenery pleasant, making it a good place for Buddhist practitioners. The grottoes are carved into the cliff, with a total of 10 caves distributed on a cliff about 70 m long east-west, among which 7 have stone-carved statues, totaling 65 small niches and 3,371 stone statues. The plane layout of the grottoes all adopts the central Buddhist altar with back screen style, with no corridor between the cave chamber and the cave entrance; the plane is square, and the cave entrance adopts imitation wooden structure techniques, carving out eave columns and architraves. Among the 7 grottoes, the earliest is Cave 5 in the middle, followed by Cave 3, Cave 2, and Cave 4; the outermost grottoes were carved later, indicating that each dynasty carved caves on both sides of existing caves, belonging to a grotto group with concentrated distribution and continuous eras. Cave 5 has an inscription from the Daye period of Sui (605-618 AD); the cave entrance is rectangular, with an interior width of 2.5 m, depth of 3 m, and height of 2.1 m; a central Buddhist altar with back screen enshrines one Buddha and two bodhisattvas, with a total of 34 statues on the east and west walls. Caves 2, 3, and 4 have similar forms; the cave doors are rectangular, with two bays carved into door lintel and door frame; the interior plane is rectangular, with depth greater than width, the cave top slightly raised, a Buddhist canopy in the center of the chamber, and the back of the Buddha statues all made into back screens直通 the cave top; various statues are on the back screens and the inner side walls of the cave. The earliest inscriptions of the above three caves are respectively: Cave 2, the 2nd year of Kaibao, Northern Song (969 AD); Cave 3, the 5th year of Xiantong, Tang (860 AD); Cave 4, the 1st year of Xiande, Later Zhou (954 AD). Cave 6 is the largest in scale with numerous statues; there is a corridor inside the cave, which for a cave chamber with large depth plays a role in structural stability. The cave chamber plane is nearly square, with a width of 10.3 m, depth of 10.65 m, and height of 5.35 m; a Buddhist altar is arranged in the center, with one Buddha, two bodhisattvas, and two disciples; the Buddha and bodhisattvas all sit cross-legged on lotus seats, with the two disciples standing on both sides. The Buddhist altar back screen evolved into four statue columns connecting the top and ground, enhancing the visual sense of depth. 1,131 statues are carved on the stone columns, 1,947 statues on the two walls of the cave chamber, and geometric pattern decorations on the cave top. The earliest date of statue inscriptions is the 1st year of Huangtong, Jin (1141 AD). In terms of statue content and carving techniques, it is more extensive and lively than in the Tang and Song periods. Caves 1 and 7 were both carved in the Ming dynasty; the caves express the content of the integration of Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism, and in terms of techniques are inferior to the other caves, showing that by the Ming dynasty, the trend of cave carving had declined. The center of the cave no longer has a Buddhist altar, but the Buddhist altar is placed at the rear wall of the cave chamber; the figure statues are stiff in form and miscellaneous in content. The Mizhi Wanfo Cave, originally named Wanfu Cave, is located on the cliff on the right bank of the Wuding River, 8 km north of Mizhi County town. It is the grotto group with the most caves and largest scale in northern Shaanxi. It was listed as a county-level cultural heritage protection unit in 1982. The construction date of Wanfo Cave is still unknown, generally believed to have been built from the Song to early Ming. The cave site is strategically located on a precipice; the cliff runs north-south along the Wuding River, about 500 m long horizontally, with a flat cliff top; the cliff layer is about 20 m above the ground and about 20 to 30 m to the cliff top. With steep cliffs and jagged rocks, the top layer protrudes outward, in a precipitous form. Wanfo Cave is built against the cliff, mainly including the Qielan Hufa Hall, Guanyin Cave, Lingguan Hall, Baiyi Cave, Guanwang Cave, and Jiutian Shengmu Cave; most statues in the existing caves have been destroyed. The main cave, Qielan Hufa Hall, has a square plane, 8 m wide, 11.6 m deep, and 4.7 m high; the front part of the cave top has 15 coffered ceiling squares, with relief-carved patterns of flowers, plants, and auspicious beasts inside; the center of the rear half is a dome top, with the Eight Trigrams in the center and a ring of small Buddha statues relief-carved around the outside. Below the front face of the cave, a rectangular stone altar base is carved, with 3 xumizuo (Sumeru pedestals) on it, and a rectangular stone altar base on each side. There are two rectangular stone columns in the cave, reaching the cave top, about 1.30 m wide on the north and south faces and about 1 m wide on the east and west faces, with small Buddhas and inscriptions carved on them; at the rock fault in the middle of the columns where statues are not suitable, colored paintings are used instead. The two walls of the cave are carved with small Buddhas of various forms and shapes, interspersed with inscriptions. The front face and north and south faces have relief Buddha statues, while the inner face has no Buddha statues. On the front face of the south column, there are 15 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, totaling 130 Buddha statues, among which the upper part has one Big-belly Buddha statue, and the lower Buddha statues are cross-legged sitting, about 0.2 m high with a 0.1 m wide base, while the small Buddha statues are 0.5 m high with a 0.1 m wide base. On the north face of the south column, the upper part has 9 rows of Buddha statues, each row with 17 horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, totaling 153 Buddha statues; the lower part has 7 rows of Buddha statues, each row with 11 horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, totaling 77 Buddha statues. On the south face of the south column, there are 18 rows of Buddha statues, each row with 16 horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, totaling 288 Buddha statues. On the front face of the north column, there are 17 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, with rows 1 to 9 having 13 statues each and rows 10 to 17 having 8 statues each, totaling 181 Buddha statues. The south face of the north column has basically the same number of rows and statues as the north face of the south column, totaling 230 Buddha statues. On the north face of the north column, there are 16 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, with each row having 11, 13, 17, or 12 statues不等, totaling 217 Buddha statues. On the front wall inside the cave, there are 12 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, with 120 statues per row, and each statue position staggered up and down per row, totaling 1,440 Buddha statues. On the north wall inside the cave, there are 18 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, with 147 statues per row, totaling 2,646 Buddha statues. On the south wall inside the cave, there are 19 rows of horizontally arranged relief Buddha statues, with 150 statues per row, totaling 2,850 Buddha statues.
